progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b01: bacteria are cells (prokaryotes, DNA in the cytoplasm, ribosomes, a peptidoglycan wall); a virus is genetic material in a protein coat with no cytoplasm and no ribosomes, which makes a host cell build new viruses; "a drug has to hit something the pathogen has and the host doesn't" (Revision 3: scene 2 refines it as harming the pathogen much more than the host, often through such a difference, after Codex check 105); "Not a cell means antibiotics are useless"; the Fleming plate. From b06: infected cells, the airway lining (via b08's plates, which b11 reuses). From b08: the infected airway cell with viruses budding from its surface. From bio-m6-b01: mutation makes a new allele by chance ("random with respect to need"); an antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria and the few already carrying a resistance allele survive and divide; "The antibiotic didn't create the allele. It changed how common it is, and that's natural selection." From bio-m5-b06a: bacteria carry plasmids. Not assumed: selective toxicity, how penicillin kills, bacterial ribosomes as a target, neuraminidase, why the flu antiviral helps most early, horizontal gene transfer by name, combination therapy, stewardship, assessing effectiveness.
progression.startsWith: Compare bacterial structures with viral replication. The video opens: Every winter, people with the flu ask their doctor for antibiotics.
progression.stopsAfter: defining selective toxicity; explaining how penicillin kills growing bacteria (wall not built, water enters, the cell bursts) and why it spares human cells (no wall); explaining that other antibiotics block bacterial ribosomes, shaped differently from ours, and showing on screen (silent since Revision 3) that some antibiotics kill while others stop growth so the immune system clears the rest; explaining why antibiotics do nothing to a virus (no wall, no ribosomes; it uses the host cell's) and how using them for a viral infection selects resistant bacteria; explaining that antivirals block a step the virus needs (oseltamivir blocks neuraminidase so new flu viruses stay stuck to the cell; others block a viral copying enzyme or entry; some block a host part the virus needs); explaining that antivirals stop new viruses but don't destroy existing ones, so the flu antiviral helps most early, while HIV treatment controls an established infection; that most antivirals are narrow, though some act on several virus families; and that they are fewer than antibiotics; explaining resistance as selection of microbes that already carry resistance, and how bacteria share resistance genes on plasmids, even between species; explaining why combination therapy prevents HIV resistance; describing sensible use (not for viral infections, not routinely in healthy farm animals, exactly as prescribed, reserve antibiotics); assessing the effectiveness of each class by selectivity, breadth and durability, with durability judged from selection and a dated figure for the size of the resistance burden.
progression.nextLesson: testing which substances stop bacteria growing on agar (route entry bio-m7-p05).

teaching.task: Antibiotics do nothing for the flu, but a flu antiviral can shorten it, if it's taken early. Why do antibiotics and antivirals work so differently, and how effective is each?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why antibiotics spare our cells (no wall; differently shaped ribosomes; 2, 3); why a wall-blocked bacterium bursts (water enters; 3); why antibiotics miss viruses (no wall, no ribosomes; the virus uses ours; 4); why antibiotics for a cold still matter (they select resistant bacteria in the body; 4); how an antiviral can work at all (many target the virus's own enzymes, some a host part the virus needs; 5); why the flu antiviral helps most early (it stops new copies, not existing viruses; 6), while HIV treatment controls an established infection (8, 10); why most are narrow and they're few (most target one virus's enzyme, though some act on several families; few safe targets; 6); how safely each class hits the pathogen (the wall and ribosome differences; oseltamivir's fit to the flu enzyme; 10); why durability depends on use (every use selects resistance; the 2021 figure shows burden, not a trend; 10); why resistance spreads (selection; plasmid sharing; 7); why three drugs stop resistance (all three at once is very unlikely; 8, 12c). Visible case: the same bacterium bursts in place; the same airway cell keeps its viruses stuck in place. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; scenes 3 (two targets, kill against stop-growth) and 10 (assess table) are the densest, so earlier tags and rows dim.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Every winter people with the flu ask for antibiotics that do nothing to the virus, while a flu antiviral can shorten the illness if taken early, so the question is why antibiotics and antivirals work so differently and how effective each is. A useful drug harms the pathogen much more than the host (selective toxicity), often by hitting something the pathogen has and our cells lack. Penicillin stops a growing bacterium building its cell wall, so it bursts, and other antibiotics block bacterial ribosomes, which differ from ours. A virus is genes in a protein coat with no wall or ribosomes, and it uses our cell's machinery, so antibiotics have nothing to hit. Antivirals block a step the virus needs with its own tools, such as the neuraminidase that cuts new flu viruses free, so they stop new viruses being made or released rather than destroying existing ones and help most early. Resistance is selected, not created: microbes that already carry resistance survive and multiply, and bacteria can share resistance genes, so for HIV, which copies itself billions of times with errors, three drugs at once mean a virus would need resistance to all three. Using drugs well slows resistance, and the drugs are assessed on how safely they hit the pathogen, how many infections they treat and how long they keep working. The memory aid is antivirals block a step the virus needs, and the drug selects resistance; it doesn't create it. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Every winter, people with the flu ask their doctor for antibiotics. The antibiotics do nothing to the flu virus. But a flu antiviral called oseltamivir can shorten the illness by about a day, if it's started within two days of the first symptoms. So why does one drug miss the virus completely, and why does the other only help if you take it early?
teaching.understandingCheck: 12a is an explain item on an invented virus and drug: why a drug that blocks a virus-only enzyme works and penicillin doesn't, and why the drug works best early (selective toxicity, no targets, timing). 12c is an explain item with numbers: why three drugs at once beat one (resistance by selection, combination therapy, the "assess" half). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reasons, givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ4-03 (p 55): "investigate and assess the effectiveness of pharmaceuticals as treatment strategies for the control of infectious disease, for example:" with its examples "antivirals" and "antibiotics". This video owns full coverage of B7-IQ4-03 apart from the "investigate" practical, which p05 carries. Verb "assess" (make a judgement of value, quality, outcomes, results or size): scene 10 states the criteria (how selectively the drug hits the pathogen, how many infections it treats, how long it keeps working) and gives a qualified judgement; attempt 2 assesses combination therapy with numbers. Verb "investigate": the hook reads trial evidence (about a day shorter, if started within two days), and scene 8 reads the history of single against combined HIV therapy as evidence.

design.visualSystem: One drug-target bench, split into two lanes. Top lane, "bacterium": `m6-bacterium-plasmid-v1.png` (a cutaway rod with a layered wall, nucleoid and plasmid) with coded target markers (small amber rings) that light on cue: "wall", "ribosomes", and, screen-only and grey, "DNA-copying enzymes" and "folate making". Bottom lane, "virus": b08's aligned airway cell set (`m7-airway-cell-v1.png`, `-infected-v1.png`) plus one new aligned partner, `m7-airway-cell-release-blocked-v1.png`, so the antiviral's effect is shown as a change in place on the same cell. A coded virus step strip runs under the cell: "enter", "copy", "build", "release", with each antiviral landing as a small coded block on its step. Each drug is a coded chip (amber for antibiotics, teal for antivirals) that slides to its lane and either locks onto a target (tick) or finds nothing (grey cross). Scene 7 reuses bio-m6-b01's coded population board (small tinted bacterium glyphs, resistance rings) and adds the new `m7-bacteria-conjugation-v1.png`. Scene 8 is a coded three-lock diagram: a virus glyph with three padlock-shaped step markers, abstract only. Scene 10 is a coded three-column assess table. No people, hands or faces: no patients, doctors, pharmacists, farmers or hospital rooms; drugs are shown as `m7-capsule-blister-blank-v1.png` (new, blank) with coded tags, never a branded pack. Scale: the bacterium and the airway cell are never drawn at one scale; each carries its own grey tag ("drawn far larger than real"). The virus particles on the airway cell are far larger than real (b08's own note). Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey labels; earlier chips dim to grey. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
